prompt: In SwiftUI, what does an animation attach to?
hint: It is not something you start, like a timer.

choices.text: A view, which plays it when it appears
choices.why: Appearing is a transition; an animation rides on a change of state.

choices.text: A change of state, saying how the screen travels to it
choices.why: Right: the state changes at once, and the animation is how the screen follows.

choices.text: A timer the view starts and stops in its body, once per frame
choices.why: Nothing in the body starts a timer; the body runs once with the new value.

choices.text: The display's refresh rate
choices.why: The refresh rate decides how many frames are drawn, not what is animated.

prompt: `WeekBar` has `.animation(.easeInOut, value: fraction)`. The phone rotates and the bar is redrawn wider. What happens?
hint: Which value does the modifier watch?

choices.text: The bar eases to its new width over 0.35 seconds
choices.why: That is what the deprecated `animation(_:)` without a value would do.

choices.text: It redraws at the new width at once, since `fraction` did not change
choices.why: Right: the animation is tied to `fraction` and nothing else.

choices.text: The fraction is recomputed and animates from zero
choices.why: The fraction is the same before and after; nothing starts from zero.

choices.text: SwiftUI refuses to rotate a view with an animation on it
choices.why: Nothing is refused; the modifier just does not apply.

prompt: A tap runs `withAnimation(.easeOut) { markDone(id) }`. Which views animate?
hint: The animation goes on the transaction.

choices.text: Only the button that was tapped
choices.why: The button is where the change started, not the only thing it changes.

choices.text: Only views with an `animation(_:value:)` modifier
choices.why: Those animate on their own; `withAnimation` reaches views without one.

choices.text: Every view whose appearance the change affects
choices.why: Right: the row, the bar and the total all move together.

choices.text: None until the next frame asks for one
choices.why: The animation is set for this change, at once.

prompt: Match each way of animating to where it is written.
hint: One on the view, one around the change.

pairs.right: Around the code that changes the state
On a view that is inserted or removed
Inside a shape whose number SwiftUI interpolates

right_distractors: In `Info.plist`, under a key for animation

prompt: While the week bar animates from two thirds to full, how many times does its body run?
hint: Who computes the frames in between?

choices.text: 21 times, once a frame at 60 Hz
choices.why: That is the frame count, but SwiftUI interpolates them without your body.

choices.text: Once, with the new value
choices.why: Right: SwiftUI interpolates the width it knows how to animate.

choices.text: Twice, once at the start and once at the end
choices.why: The body ran already for the old value; the change runs it once more.

choices.text: Not at all: animation skips the body
choices.why: The state changed, so the body runs, once.

prompt: `ProgressRing` is a `Shape` without the `animatableData` property. Inside `withAnimation`, `fraction` goes from 0.5 to 1. What does the ring do?
hint: What does the default `animatableData` return?

choices.text: It grows smoothly, because `Shape` animates its stored properties
choices.why: Not without being told: the default animatable data is empty.

choices.text: It fails to compile until `animatableData` is written
choices.why: There is a default, so it compiles; it just animates nothing.

choices.text: It jumps from half to full
choices.why: Right: `EmptyAnimatableData` means SwiftUI has nothing to interpolate.

choices.text: It fades out the half ring and fades in the full one
choices.why: A cross-fade is for a view replaced; the ring is the same view, redrawn.

prompt: The week's total changes from `"120 min"` to `"150 min"` inside an animation. What happens to the `Text` by default?
hint: A string has nothing between two values.

choices.text: It cross-fades from the old string to the new one
choices.why: Right; `.contentTransition(.numericText())` asks for rolling digits instead.

choices.text: The digits count up through 121, 122 and on to 150
choices.why: SwiftUI does not parse the string as a number.

choices.text: It cannot change while an animation runs
choices.why: It changes; how it looks while changing is the question.

choices.text: It slides in from the trailing edge
choices.why: That would be a `.move` transition, which nothing asked for here.

prompt: SwiftUI interpolates values and transitions ___: a view that starts or stops existing is handed to a transition.
hint: Lesson 3 defined it.

prompt: According to the capture, how far has an ease-out curve moved at 0.10 seconds of a 0.35-second animation? Give the progress from 0 to 1.
hint: Read the 0.10 row, the ease-out column.

prompt: Which curve suits a panel arriving because somebody tapped?
hint: It should answer at once.

choices.text: Ease-in, slow at first and fast at the end
choices.why: Slow first is a delay the person feels after tapping.

choices.text: Ease-out, fast at first
choices.why: Right: at 0.10 s it is at 0.426 where ease-in is at 0.119.

choices.text: Linear, the same speed throughout
choices.why: It works, and starts and stops abruptly; ease-out answers faster.

choices.text: None: an arriving panel should not animate
choices.why: Arriving is exactly what a short animation explains.

prompt: Since iOS 17, `withAnimation { }` with no argument uses `Animation.default`. What is still true at 0.35 seconds?
hint: The default became a spring with a response of 0.55.

choices.text: It has finished, like every animation of the default duration
choices.why: 0.35 s is the timing curves' default; a spring has no duration.

choices.text: It is still settling, short of the end
choices.why: Right: the model reaches 0.942 at 0.40 s and 0.986 at 0.55 s.

choices.text: It has overshot and is coming back
choices.why: A damping fraction of 1.0 means no bounce, so it never overshoots.

choices.text: It has not begun, since springs wait for the response
choices.why: It starts at once and rises fastest at the start.

prompt: How many frames does a 0.35-second animation get on a 120 Hz display, according to the capture?
hint: The last line.

prompt: Why does `progress(at:)` search with bisection instead of computing the curve directly from the time?
hint: The curve is defined by a parameter, not by x.

choices.text: Swift has no exponent operator
choices.why: Powers are written as products here; that is not the reason.

choices.text: Bisection is faster than any formula
choices.why: It is chosen for being simple and sure, not for speed.

choices.text: Time is the x of a point found by `s`, so the `s` for that x has to be found
choices.why: Right: find `s` where x equals the time, then answer that point's y.

choices.text: SwiftUI requires it, so that the package's numbers match its own frames exactly
choices.why: The package has nothing to do with SwiftUI; it is arithmetic.

prompt: A label has `.transition(.move(edge: .bottom))` but appears in one frame, with no movement. What is missing?
hint: A transition says how, not when or how fast.

choices.text: An animation on the change that inserts it
choices.why: Right: a transition with no animation in the transaction does nothing.

choices.text: A `.combined(with: .opacity)` beside the move
choices.why: That changes how it looks while moving; it still needs an animation to move.

choices.text: An `@Namespace` shared with the label
choices.why: A namespace is for matched geometry, section 06.

choices.text: `animatableData` on the label
choices.why: That is for interpolating a shape's numbers, not for inserting a view.

prompt: Which transition lets a new row arrive from the top and a deleted one leave by fading?
hint: One way in, another way out.

choices.text: `.move(edge: .top).combined(with: .opacity)`
choices.why: That does both on the way in and both on the way out.

choices.text: `.slide`
choices.why: It moves in from the leading edge and out to the trailing one.

choices.text: `.asymmetric(insertion: .move(edge: .top), removal: .opacity)`
choices.why: Right: insertion and removal each get their own.

choices.text: `.scale`
choices.why: That grows from nothing and shrinks to nothing.

prompt: A list animates a removal and an insertion every time a session's minutes are edited. What is the likely cause?
hint: What tells a list that a row is the same row?

choices.text: The edit is not inside `withAnimation`
choices.why: Without an animation nothing would animate at all.

choices.text: The list needs `.transition(.identity)` on each row
choices.why: The list decides its own row animations; the cause is identity.

choices.text: The rows' identity changes with the edit, so the list sees a new row
choices.why: Right, as with an id derived from the contents: lesson 8's stable `id` fixes it.

choices.text: Lists cannot animate an edit in place, so every edit is shown as a swap
choices.why: A row with the same identity is updated in place and its values change.

prompt: What does `matchedGeometryEffect` link between the two views?
hint: Apple's documentation separates geometry from rendering.

choices.text: Their colours and fonts as well as their frames
choices.why: Rendering is left to each view's own transition.

choices.text: Their frames, so one seems to move to the other's place
choices.why: Right: geometry only; each view still fades with its own transition.

choices.text: Their state, so changing one changes the other
choices.why: State is not shared by this modifier.

choices.text: Their identity, so SwiftUI sees one view
choices.why: They stay two views; their frames are interpolated.

prompt: A bug selects two days at once and two capsules are drawn with the same id, both as sources. What does the documentation say happens?
hint: It asks for exactly one source in a group.

choices.text: SwiftUI keeps the first one and ignores the second
choices.why: No rule picks the first; the documentation calls it undefined.

choices.text: The build fails with a duplicate-id error
choices.why: Nothing checks this at compile time.

choices.text: The results are undefined
choices.why: Right, which is why `selected` holds one day and never two.

choices.text: Both capsules slide to the middle of the two days
choices.why: There is no averaging rule in the documentation.

prompt: Put the day picker's slide in order, from tap to the capsule under the new day.
hint: Tap, change, remove and insert, interpolate.
items: The student taps another day's button
The body runs and draws the capsule under the new day only
SwiftUI sees one "selection" removed and one inserted
It interpolates the frame from the old day to the new one

prompt: What does Apple's documentation say an interface should do when `accessibilityReduceMotion` is true?
hint: It is about one kind of animation.

choices.text: Remove every animation and every transition
choices.why: It asks to avoid large ones; feedback can stay.

choices.text: Avoid large animations, especially ones simulating 3D
choices.why: Right: in its words, "especially those that simulate the third dimension".

choices.text: Slow every animation down to half speed
choices.why: Slower movement is still movement.

choices.text: Show a warning before animating
choices.why: Nothing in the documentation asks for a warning.

prompt: With Reduce Motion on, why does the planner keep the week bar's animation?
hint: Which movement does the setting worry about?

choices.text: The setting does not apply to shapes
choices.why: It applies to any motion; the bar is kept by choice.

choices.text: Because removing it would break the package's tests on Linux
choices.why: The package's tests know nothing of animation.

choices.text: It grows in place and confirms the tap, without travelling
choices.why: Right: removing motion is not removing feedback.

choices.text: The system animates it whatever the app asks
choices.why: That is true of the system's own sheet, not of the app's bar.

prompt: Which of these would make the planner animate nothing when the bar changes? Choose all that apply.
hint: An animation needs a change and a way to travel.

choices.text: `withAnimation(nil) { markDone(id) }` with no `animation(_:value:)` on the bar
choices.why: Yes: a change with no animation, and nothing on the bar to add one.

choices.text: `.animation(.easeInOut, value: fraction)` on the bar, any tap
choices.why: No: that animates the bar whenever the fraction changes.

choices.text: Drawing the bar as a `Shape` with no `animatableData`
choices.why: Yes: the shape has nothing to interpolate, so it jumps.

choices.text: Running on a 120 Hz display instead of 60
choices.why: No: that draws twice the frames of the same animation.

prompt: The week bar goes from 120 of 180 minutes to all 180 with ease-in-out. What percentage full is it at 0.175 seconds, according to the capture?
